1.e4 c5 2.d4.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith–Morra Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.d4.background: The gambit proper arises after 2...cxd4 3.c3 and is named after Pierre Morra (1900–1969) of France and Ken Smith (1930–1999) of the Dallas Chess Club. Around 1950 Morra published a booklet and several articles on it, and Smith wrote a total of nine books and forty-nine articles on the gambit.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4.strategy: Takes the central pawn with the flank pawn, the exchange 1...c5 was played for. White now has to decide between a quick recapture that costs time and a pawn sacrifice for development.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 e6.strategy: Declines to take on d4 and so gives up the point of 1...c5, the trade of a flank pawn for White's central pawn. White decides how to resolve the tension, usually keeping a lead in space against a cramped set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre before Black is developed. After 3.exd5 Qxd5 the queen is driven back by Nc3 with tempo, and White leads in development against an open centre, while Black's flank pawn has still not traded for a central one.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3.background: An early appearance was Kieseritzky against Vitzthum in 1846. The gambit then went largely unplayed for the next century, apart from a few games in the 1920s and 1930s, until its revival in the 1950s. Today it is popular at club level and played occasionally by masters.
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3.strategy: Offers a pawn for a lead in development: after ...dxc3 and Nxc3 White has moved both centre pawns, so both bishops are free, while Black needs two pawn moves before its own bishops can come out. White plays for open c- and d-files and a quick attack, Black for the extra pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4.strategy: Regains the pawn at once and centralises the queen, but ...Nc6 attacks it with a developing move, so White spends a second tempo on the queen. Black gets the initiative and neutralises White's first-move advantage, while White's position stays sound, only slow.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nf3.name: Sicilian Defence: Morphy Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nf3.background: Popular in the nineteenth century; one of its earliest appearances was von der Lasa against Mayet in 1857. Paul Morphy played it frequently, aiming for open Sicilian positions.
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nf3.strategy: Prepares to retake on d4 with the knight, so the queen is not driven back by ...Nc6, and if Black allows it an ordinary open Sicilian arises. But Black can hold the pawn with ...e5: the knight cannot take it, because ...Qa5+ wins a piece, so White ends up gambiting a pawn after all.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.f4.name: Sicilian Defence: Halasz Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.f4.strategy: Neither takes the pawn back nor develops a piece, and it loosens the e1-h4 diagonal. Black develops with tempo, even bringing the queen out with check, and White has to spend time winning the pawn back. Sound enough, but slower than the direct recaptures.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3.strategy: Accepts the gambit: Black wins a pawn and has a d- and e-pawn against White's lone e-pawn in the centre, but must now finish development against open lines. The task is to untangle safely and, ideally, to keep the extra pawn into the endgame.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Declined, Alapin Formation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 Nf6.strategy: Declines by hitting the e-pawn and steers towards a quiet c3 Sicilian: White can drive the knight to d5 and retake on d4, building a pawn centre on d4 and e5 that Black attacks with pieces. Black avoids the pawn-down fight and can use the same preparation against the quiet 2.c3.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 d5.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Declined, Scandinavian Formation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 d5.strategy: Meets the gambit with a central strike: after the exchanges the extra pawn is gone and White has an isolated pawn on d4, but the queen on d5 will lose time to Nc3. A sound way to avoid the theory that leads to a roughly level game.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 e5.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Declined, Centre Formation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 e5.strategy: Tries to hold d4, but White simply retakes with the c-pawn, and after the recapture on d4 the knights develop and win the pawn back. Black avoids the gambit but gets nothing for it: the pawn goes anyway, and White's pieces come out with tempo.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 d3.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Declined, Push Variation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 d3.strategy: Hands the pawn straight back, so Black never has to defend against a gambit. The price is a passive position: White takes on d3, builds pawns on c4 and e4 that clamp d5, and has more space, though Black stays flexible and sound.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 Qa5.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Declined, Wing Formation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 Qa5.strategy: Pins the c3 pawn to the king, so White cannot retake on d4 with it, and keeps the pawn for now. But the queen comes out early, White simply develops and regains the pawn, and Black has spent time that development needed.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 d3 4.c4.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Declined, Dubois Variation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 d3 4.c4.strategy: Puts the centre before the pawn: the black pawn on d3 is attacked twice and has no defender, and with pawns on c4 and e4 White also clamps the d5 square. White regains the pawn with a space advantage, a solid and slightly better position with little risk.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 d3 4.Bxd3.strategy: Wins the pawn back with a developing move. The c3 pawn still blocks the knight's best square, which costs White time, but the bishop is active, the centre stays White's and Black has little to show for declining the gambit.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 d3 4.Qxd3.strategy: Regains the pawn with the queen, which then blocks the king's bishop and leaves the c3 pawn in front of the knight. Material is level and nothing hangs, but White's development is clumsy, and Black can complete its own without difficulty.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3.strategy: Retakes with a developing move. White has now moved both centre pawns, so both bishops are free, and the pawn bought quick pieces and play on the open c- and d-files; Black is a pawn up but has no piece out and two bishops locked behind pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nf3.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Danish Variation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nf3.strategy: Offers a second pawn: after ...cxb2 the recapture Bxb2 gives White a bishop on the long diagonal and quick development, but only for two pawns. That is too much to give for the compensation; Black simply takes and keeps a clear material edge.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.bxc3.strategy: Recaptures with the b-pawn, which leaves isolated a- and c-pawns and puts a pawn on the knight's best square. White has given a pawn and gets no lead in development for it: the cost of the gambit with none of its compensation.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6.strategy: The most flexible reply: it develops a piece and controls d4 and e5, so White cannot push the e-pawn yet, and Black can later develop the king's bishop without Qd4 hitting b4 and g7. Black starts the task of untangling against White's lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 d6.strategy: Controls e5 so White cannot gain space there, and opens the diagonal of the queen's bishop. It builds a compact pawn wall, but it commits the d-pawn before any piece is out, so Black still has all of its development to do against White's lead.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 e6.strategy: Opens the king's bishop and covers d5, a solid reply that also softens the bishop's pressure on f7 in advance. The king stays in the centre, though, and a knight sacrifice on d5 that opens the e-file is always a tactical idea for White.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 g6.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Fianchetto Defence
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 g6.strategy: Heads for a fianchetto, where the bishop on g7 pressures the knight on c3 along the long diagonal. Sound but slow: a flank pawn move while White is already developing, and if ...e6 follows as well the dark squares around the king become weak.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 d6 5..strategy: Natural development: the knight covers d4 and e5 and clears the way to castle. White has no need to hurry, since each developing move adds to the lead for the pawn, while Black still has to find a safe formation for its pieces.

Puts the bishop on the diagonal to f7 at once, where only the king guards the pawn, and prepares to castle. Black has no piece out yet, so it must watch f7 and finish its development before the extra pawn means anything.
Develops the bishop to a square that bears on a7 and covers d4. But it leaves d2 empty, so ...Qa5 pins the c3 knight to the king and makes e4 harder to hold, and the bishop adds nothing against f7.

Opens the king's bishop and builds a solid d6-e6 pawn pair that covers d5 and e5. Black aims to complete development and castle before White's lead can be used, accepting a slightly passive position for the extra pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 d6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Fianchetto Defence
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 d6 5..strategy: Heads for a fianchetto and a bishop aimed at the knight on c3. Sound, but a slow flank pawn move while White's pieces come out, and the white bishop will soon target f7 with no pawn yet in its way.
Develops the queenside knight, covering d4 and e5 and keeping the pawn structure flexible. With the d-pawn on d6, though, Bb5 would pin the knight against the king, so Black has to be ready for that.

The natural developing move: the bishop controls d5, pressures the e6 pawn and clears the way to castle. White's lead in development grows, while Black's solid pawns leave the queen's bishop boxed in behind e6.
Develops the bishop to a square that covers d4 and bears on a7. It leaves d2 empty, so ...Qa5 pins the c3 knight against the king and makes e4 hard to hold, and White does not yet press on e6 or f7.

A solid, unambitious development: the bishop is safe and castling is quick. But it leaves the attacking diagonal, so the compensation for the pawn shrinks and Black has time to finish its own development.

Develops the knight with pressure on e4 and prepares castling. Black's fight is to get the king safe while the extra pawn is still on the board, and the solid pawn pair on d6 and e6 gives the pieces cover to do it.

Takes b5 away from White's knight and bishop and prepares ...b5 to drive the bishop back, building queenside counterplay. It is a flank pawn move, though, so Black's king stays in the centre a move longer than with a developing move.

Develops the queenside knight to the centre, covering d4 and e5, while the d6-e6 pawn pair keeps the position closed to White's pieces. The set-up is flexible, with the king's knight free to choose its square, at the price of one more move before castling.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 e6 5..strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square without committing the bishop, which keeps its options open. Black has no piece out yet and must choose a pawn structure while White gets ready to castle.

Develops the bishop at once, pressuring e6 and controlling d5 while White heads for quick castling. Placing it before the knight shows Black what is coming, and Black can use the time to gain queenside space.

Develops the bishop to a square where it supports e4 and prepares quick castling. But it stands on the d-file where the rooks want to play, and it gives up the pressure on e6, so the pawn is less well paid for.

Takes b5 away from the knight and bishop and prepares ...b5 to gain queenside space with tempo against the bishop. It is slow while White leads in development, but the pawns on e6 and a6 give Black a flexible position with several plans.

Develops the queenside knight first, covering d4 and e5, instead of spending a move on a flank pawn. Black meets White's lead in development with a piece of its own and keeps its pawn structure flexible, though the king stays in the centre for now.

Frees the queen's bishop and takes e5 under control, a solid base for a compact pawn centre. It is a pawn move while White's pieces are ready, and the pawn on e6 stays under the bishop's eye, so Black still has to catch up in development.
Completes the kingside development, so castling is next. White's pieces bear on the open centre and the c- and d-files, while Black's queen's bishop and king's knight are still at home.

Takes b5 away from the black pawn: after 6...b5 7.axb5 axb5 the a-file opens and the a8 rook hangs to 8.Rxa8. It hampers Black's usual plan, but it is a flank move that adds nothing to White's development, which is the compensation for the pawn.

Guards e4, so the knight on c3 is free to move, and vacates d1 for a rook, the way White wants to use the open d-file. The king's knight is still at home, though, so Black can use the time to expand on the queenside.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 e6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Taimanov Formation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 e6 5..strategy: Develops the knight where it guards d5 and avoids ...Nf6, which would offer White's e-pawn a free push. But it blocks the king's bishop, and a white bishop on g5 can then force Black to weaken the kingside to keep developing.

Carries out the point of ...a6 at once: the pawn drives the bishop back and wins queenside space with tempo, and the bishop on b7 can then press on e4. The king is still in the centre, and the advanced pawns give White sacrificial targets on b5 and d5.
Brings the queenside knight to the centre, where it covers d4 and e5, and keeps ...b5 in reserve. The set-up is compact and flexible, but the king is still uncastled and White's bishop presses on e6.

Takes control of e5 and frees the queen's bishop, reaching the same compact d6-e6 structure as the lines where ...d6 comes first. Black has spent a move on a pawn rather than a piece, so development must now catch up.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 e6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Kan Formation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 e6 5..strategy: Prevents Nb5 and Bb5 and prepares queenside expansion, keeping all pawn structures and the knight's squares open. No piece comes out, though, so White uses the time to bring the bishop out and castle.

Develops the queenside knight at once, covering d4 and e5, so that Black meets White's lead in development with a piece rather than a pawn move. The structure stays flexible, but while the king is in the centre Black must watch for sacrifices on d5.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.strategy: The standard development: the knight covers d4 and e5, prepares castling and keeps the bishop's square open. Black must untangle against a lead in development, with the extra pawn as its compensation.

Aims the bishop at f7 at once, where only the king defends it, so Black normally closes the diagonal with a pawn before developing further. White gets quick pressure and early castling for little cost.

Develops the bishop before the knights, so the king's knight keeps its options, and bears on a7. But it leaves d2 empty, so ...Qa5 pins the c3 knight against the king, and the pressure on f7 that is the point of the gambit comes later.

Blocks the bishop's diagonal to f7 with a pawn that also covers d5, and opens the king's bishop. It is the solid answer; the pawn on e6 now faces the bishop, and Black's queen's bishop is still shut in behind the d7 pawn.

Frees the queen's bishop and takes e5 under control, building a compact pawn centre. The pawn on f7 is guarded by the king alone for now, but one attacker cannot win it, and Black keeps a free hand over how to develop the kingside.

Prepares ...b5 to gain queenside space with tempo against the bishop and keeps White's pieces off b5. It is a flank pawn move while Black has only one piece out and f7 is under the bishop's eye, so it gives White time to develop.

Completes the kingside development and prepares castling, reaching the main set-up of the gambit by the other move order. White has the more active pieces, and Black has to decide how to arrange its pawns and bishops.

Develops the bishop to a square that covers d4 and bears on b6 and a7, so ...Nd4 and ...Qb6 both simply lose material. It adds no pressure on e6 and leaves the king's knight at home, so Black gets time to settle its pieces.
Hangs the bishop: nothing defends g5, so Black simply takes it with the queen and White has nothing to show for the piece.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Scheveningen Formation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.strategy: Opens the diagonal of the queen's bishop and controls e5 with a compact d6-e6 pawn pair, a solid way to arrange the pawns. Black is ready to castle and to free the position later with a central break, and the extra pawn promises a good endgame if the attack is survived.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Siberian Variation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.strategy: Puts the queen on the diagonal that eyes h2. It sets a trap: after ...Nf6, castling and Qe2, the knight jump ...Ng4 makes the natural h3 lose decisive material to ...Nd4, with Qh2 mate threatened.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Morphy Defence
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.strategy: Develops the bishop to an active square, eyeing f2 and the white king's shelter. The price is that the bishop becomes a target for a knight on a4, and the king stays in the centre a little longer.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Paulsen Formation
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.strategy: Prevents Nb5 and Bb5 and prepares queenside space with ...b5, keeping both bishops' routes open. It is slower than a developing move, so Black relies on the solid pawns to hold while the king is uncastled.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Pin Defence
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.strategy: Pins the knight on c3 to the king, so it cannot jump to d5 or b5, and prepares to trade the bishop for it and damage White's pawns. Black removes an active piece, but spends another tempo on the bishop while White castles and keeps the initiative.
The main reply: it opens the king's bishop and, once the white bishop reaches c4, shields f7 behind a pawn. Black reaches the position where the choice of set-up is made, with a solid pawn on e6.
Controls e5 and frees the queen's bishop, a classical and flexible set-up. It leaves f7 guarded only by the king for now, so Black has to take care of that square once the bishop arrives on c4.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Fianchetto Defence
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.strategy: A small sideline: the bishop on g7 will pressure the knight on c3, but the pawn move weakens the dark squares around the king, and White can open the kingside with the h-pawn. It also makes ...e6 unwise, since the dark squares would be too weak.
The bishop goes to its best diagonal at once, aiming at f7 where only the king defends it, and clears the way to castle. Black has to deal with that pressure before anything else.

Pins the c6 knight against the king, since the d-pawn has left d7, and threatens to double Black's pawns by taking it. But White is a pawn down, so trading its bishop for a knight helps Black, and the bishop leaves the diagonal to f7.
Develops the bishop to a square that covers d4 and bears on a7. But it leaves d2 empty, so ...Qa5 pins the c3 knight against the king, and White gives up pressure on f7 for a quiet developing move.

Closes the diagonal to f7 with a pawn and sets up the compact d6-e6 structure; the position is the same as with the other move order. Black plans to finish development and castle, trusting the solid structure to absorb the pressure.

Delays ...e6 so that the queen's bishop can leave first, for g4, instead of being locked behind the e6 pawn, and takes b5 away from White's pieces. The cost is that f7 stays under the bishop's pressure in the meantime.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted, Fianchetto Defence
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.strategy: Fianchetto: the bishop on g7 pressures c3 and Black can castle quickly. But f7 is still under the bishop's eye, Black lacks the flexible ...e6 structure, and playing ...e6 later would weaken the dark squares.

The Morra bishop: it eyes e6 and the d5 square, where a knight sacrifice can tear the position open. White is a pawn down but ahead in development, with open lines for the rooks; Black must develop accurately to keep the extra pawn.

Puts the bishop on a square where it supports e4 and prepares quick castling. But it stands on the d-file that the rooks want and leaves e6 and f7 alone, so White's compensation for the pawn is thinner.

Attacks the queen at once, and the knight on f3 supports the bishop, so ...Qa5 does not win it. Black has to answer the question first, usually by trading the bishop or weakening the kingside, which costs White a move for little gain.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nf3 e5.strategy: Punishes the move order: the e5 pawn guards d4, so Black keeps the extra pawn instead of drifting into a regular Open Sicilian, and 4.Nxe5? loses a knight to ...Qa5+. The cost is a fixed centre and a d5 square no pawn can cover.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nf3 d6.strategy: Lets White recapture with the knight on d4, reaching a normal position in which the d-file is open and the knight stands in the centre. Black returns the pawn, but the move order has gained White nothing and ...d6 is a solid, flexible set-up covering e5 and c5.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and guards d4 a second time, so White recapturing with the knight can be challenged at once. Black gives the pawn back for an ordinary open game, and White's move order has gained nothing.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nf3 e5 4.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: Morphy Gambit, Andreaschek Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nf3 e5 4.c3.strategy: A gambit in the Morra spirit: if Black takes on c3 and White recaptures with the knight, White is a pawn down for quicker development and open lines. If Black does not take, the c3 pawn attacks d4 at once, so Black has to decide immediately.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nf3 e5 4.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop toward f7 and keeps the option of c3 for the next move. It does not yet challenge the pawn on d4, which the e5 pawn guards, so Black gets a move to consolidate the extra pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nf3 e5 4.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop to guard e4 and prepare castling, but does nothing about the pawn on d4, which the e5 pawn holds. White is a pawn down with no plan yet to win it back.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6.strategy: Wins a tempo by attacking the queen, which must move again while Black develops. Black gets the initiative and takes the sting out of White's first-move advantage.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4, which the queen alone defends, and prepares ...Nc6 with the same gain of time on the queen. Black develops with threats instead of defending anything, and White's queen has to look after the pawn as well as itself.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 d6.strategy: Solid and flexible: the pawn frees the queen's bishop and takes e5 and c5 under control. It lets White choose how to develop before the queen is attacked, so Black gives up the immediate gain of time on it.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1.strategy: The plain retreat: the queen is safe on its home square and keeps White's development flexible, and the pawn is regained. The time lost to ...Nc6 is real, so Black stands slightly better, but White has no weaknesses and a sound game.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd3.strategy: Keeps the queen in the centre instead of going home, but ...Nb4 attacks it again, and it must go to a square that still guards c2 or ...Nxc2+ forks king and rook. White may lose more time than with the plain retreat.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qa4.strategy: Moves the queen with an attack on the c6 knight, but two pawns guard it, so the attack threatens little. The queen no longer defends e4, so Black gains a tempo with ...Nf6.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a second tempo by attacking the e4 pawn, which nothing defends yet. White has to spend another move on it, and Black keeps the lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1 e5.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn and gives the knight on c6 a firm support. Black gets space and a solid game, at the price of a hole on d5 and a d-pawn that is backward on the half-open d-file, where White's queen and pieces can aim for it.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and to pressure the centre from a distance. A flexible and sound set-up, but it does not attack e4, so White gets a free move to finish development and the lead in time shrinks.

1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1 Nf6 5.name: Sicilian Defence: Coles Sicilian Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1 Nf6 5.strategy: Offers the e4 pawn, which the knight on f6 already attacks, for a bishop aimed at f7. A gambit with little behind it: Black can simply take the pawn, and White has to make the pressure on f7 count at once.

Defends the attacked pawn with a developing move, so the queen's lost tempi stop costing White anything. White stands slightly behind in development but sound: Black has the central pawn majority, White a queenside one, and the game is level to a small edge for Black.

Defends e4 with the bishop and keeps the knights flexible. The bishop blocks the queen's file and can be harassed by ...Nb4, so White spends yet more time on a piece that is not placed ideally, and Black keeps the easier game.
